<span id="paper-agent-research-frontier-opd-63269744" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4da2b7b9e7379237">Why does Frontier-OPD ask teachers to take over only at selected states instead of generating all training trajectories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afrontier-opd">Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full teacher interaction is expensive, and imitating smooth teacher trajectories may miss student bottlenecks. Frontier-OPD finds teachable frontiers from student-visited states, briefly bridges with the teacher, then hands control back. Savings must be accompanied by verifying that the student can continue after the bridge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the student repeatedly gets stuck opening a door after finding its key, test a short teacher intervention there rather than having the teacher finish every task from scratch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32802v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.32802-frontier-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4da2b7b9e7379237">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:frontier-opd" data-paper-title="Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-98ef87ac80ac6218">Why average student–teacher disagreement within trajectories and then across trajectories instead of across node visits?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afrontier-opd">Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Loops repeatedly visit states; counting each visit as independent evidence lets one circling path dominate. Two-stage averaging balances trajectory weight. Representative histories then support real teacher-bridge trials. Signed disagreement for ranking differs from agreement for validation; a high node score does not guarantee takeover helps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three visits at disagreement ten in one trajectory and one zero in another give a balanced score of five. Visit averaging gives 7.5 and overweights the loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32802v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.32802-frontier-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98ef87ac80ac6218">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:frontier-opd" data-paper-title="Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-538f695379155fc1">Why use different criteria for high-ranking frontier nodes and valid teacher bridges?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afrontier-opd">Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Signed teacher–student disagreement prioritizes where to spend limited teacher budget. Bridge validation compares actual takeover plus student continuation to an equally long historical window, requiring valid replay and nondecreasing agreement. Prioritization is not training-data admission; a high-ranked node does not prove teaching works.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>High disagreement may warrant a trial even if the student still cannot continue after takeover. Do not add that failed bridge to training merely because it ranked high.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32802v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.32802-frontier-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-538f695379155fc1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:frontier-opd" data-paper-title="Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c6a4f6a4fdc8378a">How are windows compared when the bridge is shorter than K, and can its continuation enter training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afrontier-opd">Frontier-OPD: Discovering the Edge of Agent Capability and Teaching Agents to Go Beyond</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compare equal windows of actual bridge length plus H. Require valid replay, nonterminal handoff, and complete continuation; accept bridge responses only when agreement does not decrease. Student continuation used for validation cannot enter training, and retain repeated responses separately. The local path is only the L1 numeric protocol, without the trainer or full experience pool.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If K caps the bridge at two turns but the teacher uses one, compare windows of one plus H. Do not use a longer historical window or train on the validation continuation as teacher demonstration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32802v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.32802-frontier-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c6a4f6a4fdc8378a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:asteroid" data-paper-title="Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-asteroid-1bdda102" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-98484c774b0b30a3">Why might imitating expert successes be insufficient in a hidden-task environment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aasteroid">Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The student tries imperfect actions and encounters information and states absent from smooth expert paths. ASTEROID combines student exploration with expert success to cover actual uncertainty. Exploration uses visible interaction, and expert training information remains isolated rather than exposing hidden tasks or solutions during evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The expert takes the right path immediately, while the student tries the wrong door first. Learning only the expert&#x27;s opening does not show the student how to use observed failure information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30105v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.30105-asteroid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98484c774b0b30a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:asteroid" data-paper-title="Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bf60456848f6e9e7">Why let the student explore before learning the expert&#x27;s full successful trajectory for the same hidden task?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aasteroid">Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An expert knows the hidden goal, so a direct success omits the context of continuing after mistakes. Condition expert-action prediction on the student&#x27;s actual history, teaching task inference from observations and rewards. The hidden goal stays unavailable during deployment, and student exploration actions are not automatically correct labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After the student searches two wrong rooms, the expert&#x27;s success on the same task can teach how to narrow the search from that history rather than merely memorize a direct opening.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30105v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.30105-asteroid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bf60456848f6e9e7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:asteroid" data-paper-title="Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8ee47c30c993734e">Why shouldn&#x27;t cross-episode BAMDP conditioning and generic POMDP takeover be reduced to single-step DAgger?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aasteroid">Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed-latent BAMDP accumulates task knowledge across episodes and pairs it with an expert episode on the same task. A generic POMDP hands over at an intermediate student state. Complete expert traces and context are defining; a single current-action label discards them. Deployment cannot keep invoking a latent-aware expert.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the hidden door stays the same across three attempts, first-round failure informs the next. If the door changes each round, the same cross-episode history no longer conveys that knowledge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30105v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.30105-asteroid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8ee47c30c993734e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:asteroid" data-paper-title="Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1830851d2191bbd">How does the local single-step three-door diagnostic preserve complete expert trajectories, and what are its limits?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aasteroid">Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each door choice is a complete one-step episode, so expert length one reflects the environment rather than general simplification of a multistep method. A real small Transformer is supervised only on the terminal expert query, not student-history actions. Deployment starts with empty history and no expert; there is no general POMDP or robotics comparison.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An incorrect student attempt stays in context, but loss does not train it to repeat the error. The correct expert action is stored separately as the training target.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 保留的定义机制与缩小边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30105v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.30105-asteroid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1830851d2191bbd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rsipo" data-paper-title="RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-rsipo-71b84017" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-28a01f8794a0c2d3">Why does RSIPO update old skills as the policy improves?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arsipo">RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Older skills reflect older policies and can become redundant, obsolete, or worse than direct solving by the current student. RSIPO forms skills from current trajectories and tests same-start gains, allowing skills and policy to co-evolve. Assistance is not inherently beneficial; keep independent controls and do not include original answers in evaluation input.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An early skill uses a long search while the current policy finds evidence directly. Re-measure instead of forcing an older, potentially slower skill.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15772">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.15772-rsipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-28a01f8794a0c2d3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rsipo" data-paper-title="RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9728e8966646598d">Why shrink estimated skill gains by reliability before setting skill-enhanced teacher distillation weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arsipo">RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Some skills are useless or worse than the student, so equal trust can transfer regressions. Independent controls and same-start replay estimate utility differences. Shrink noisy estimates toward the group mean and use more reliable gains to adjust distillation trust. Skill reward and shrinkage-based trust have distinct roles; invalid replay is not paired evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One lucky successful trial merits shrinkage because the gain is uncertain. A skill that works repeatedly in same-start controls can receive more distillation weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15772">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.15772-rsipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9728e8966646598d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rsipo" data-paper-title="RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f6ffb006746e4a09">How does dynamic skill–policy co-updating differ from a fixed offline skill library in freshness?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arsipo">RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed library stabilizes retrieval conditions but preserves experience from old policies and tasks. Co-updating builds skills from current trajectories and tests benefits with independent controls and same-start replay, tracking changing ability. It adds nonstationarity and evaluation cost. Update counts are not benefit or evidence of a reliable teacher.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a policy learns a shorter evidence path, a new skill can reflect it. A fixed old library may continue recommending the obsolete path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15772">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.15772-rsipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f6ffb006746e4a09">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rsipo" data-paper-title="RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-21d3144e7a542768">Does the local project have an RSIPO adapter, real skill replay, and policy training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arsipo">RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It records the specification and cost decision only, with no paper adapter, metrics, or GPU pass. An implementation must preserve current-policy skills, valid same-start replay, independent controls, and training/test separation. Another skill operator or fixed rule cannot substitute for full RSIPO or Evolve integration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A working GRPO trainer does not establish skill utility estimation or reliability-weighted OPSD. Without those, the algorithm is not implemented.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 边界与后续触发条件. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15772">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.15772-rsipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21d3144e7a542768">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evo2" data-paper-title="Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-evo2-2bf44b34" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e0e1fab4556cc465">Why does Evo2 want proposal and reflection abilities to learn from search experience?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevo2">Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed evolver repeats the same proposal habits and may persist with low-value or invalid changes. Evo2 trains generation and reflection from search experience while freezing the task executor to clarify what updates. New search versions do not mean the base executor trained, and benefits still require independent execution evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Train a proposer to learn from repeated invalid structures without necessarily changing the weights of the model that executes the tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13025">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13025-evo2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e0e1fab4556cc465">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evo2" data-paper-title="Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4e5c6f6a3a4054b6">Why does training the Proposer and Reflector with a frozen executor improve the evolver itself?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevo2">Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The task model stays fixed, but parameters of the policies that propose and repair harnesses change. Effective edit trajectories provide training signals for both roles. Improvement targets how harnesses are changed, not just the candidates. Keep actions still earn zero; unchanged proposals are not successful innovations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same executor handles tasks, but the trained proposer chooses better log compression and the reflector fixes bad hooks. The gain comes from changing the improvement process.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13025">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13025-evo2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4e5c6f6a3a4054b6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evo2" data-paper-title="Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dae08c347acff56e">How does tree-parent weight ε+|V−1/2| differ from favoring only high-success nodes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevo2">Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It favors values far from the midpoint and retains a fixed root sampling share. This allocates search rather than monotonically choosing higher scores. Cross-branch crossover and the reflector also produce new harnesses; greedy champion-only search is not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>V=0 and V=1 are both farther from the center than V=1/2, so parents are not selected simply in descending success-rate order.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13025">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13025-evo2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dae08c347acff56e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evo2" data-paper-title="Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-589b7fe7e2d4b7ca">How are keep rewards, role advantages, and truncated tokens handled in the loss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevo2">Evo2: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keep earns zero. For each role, subtract the group mean reward. Normalize token loss by fixed Lmax and mask truncated outputs so length does not alter training scale. The real local path has specific environment and resource limits: a 7B policy/executor plus frozen copies is not presumed to fit A30 or constitute the full paper benchmark.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not supervise an incomplete truncated tail as a correct edit. Averaging by the shorter actual length would also alter the original training weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 结果、验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13025">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13025-evo2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-589b7fe7e2d4b7ca">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-race-11c5fa7f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-126077c5cb720dd9">Why does RACE remove reasoning that does not help an agent&#x27;s trajectory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long-horizon agents generate much reasoning that repeats information or does not affect later actions, yet adds training and inference load. RACE reduces redundancy while preserving behavioral support. Shorter is not inherently better: deletion can remove needed context, so check downstream effects rather than using word count alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeating a goal without changing later choices may be redundant. A brief note with a critical path cannot be removed just because it is short.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-126077c5cb720dd9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-98ccf35fdf26f763">Why check likelihood changes for all later original actions when deleting a turn&#x27;s reasoning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An unchanged immediate action does not show earlier reasoning is irrelevant to later planning. After tentative deletion, evaluate later actions in the affected context and proceed only if changes stay within tolerance. Accepted deletions persist for later compression. Checking only the current turn misses long-range dependencies, and removed token counts are not task success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reasoning may record a safety restriction while the current action only reads a file. A later deletion relies on that restriction, so a current-turn-only check can wrongly remove critical reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98ccf35fdf26f763">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4be62e7f3db5d3ea">How does a reasoning loss mask differ from actually deleting training context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A mask removes supervision for deemed-removable tokens, while other actions train under prescribed conditions. Deleting context directly changes later prediction distributions. RACE also supervises early closing and keeps denominators for all original policy tokens and turns; rescaling by amount removed would silently change the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If half the reasoning supervision is removed, still normalize by original token count to avoid inadvertently doubling the weight of remaining actions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4be62e7f3db5d3ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-202711996a37bca1">How do real trajectory requirements and the local bounded-calculator run limit conclusions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real training data need an environment, revision, split, and reasoning/action/observation records. QA rows are not tool trajectories. The local calculator actually samples actions and runs SFT/on-policy updates, but is L1 mechanism evidence only. A few successes under one seed do not replicate ScienceWorld or four-environment RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Calling two real calculation tools demonstrates interactive training, not long-horizon web or embodied capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-202711996a37bca1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:depgpo" data-paper-title="Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-depgpo-58f41b1f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5869340756f1992c">Why track command dependencies in DEPGPO when terminal tasks only yield final success or failure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adepgpo">Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A long trace contains many file reads and writes; terminal reward cannot identify which commands produced the result. DEPGPO connects verification to earlier effective work through actual dependencies. Dataflow is not causal contribution of every command, and missing records or verifier side effects require explicit boundaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Trace the source file read by a final test to the command that wrote it. Unrelated directory browsing should not get equal credit just because it appeared in the trace.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03634">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03634-depgpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5869340756f1992c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:depgpo" data-paper-title="Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6b464bc6f959c9dc">Why connect file reads to the writers of the still-current versions in a command dependency graph?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adepgpo">Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reads consume the version active at that moment. Earlier overwritten writes may not affect the final artifact. Trace backward from verifier-checked outputs to connect data-contributing commands to the result and avoid sharing terminal advantage with unrelated steps. Graph construction needs trusted execution records, not guesses from command text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If a configuration is written and overwritten before a test reads it, the unused old write should not receive the same credit as the current version.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03634">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03634-depgpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6b464bc6f959c9dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:depgpo" data-paper-title="Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-10cd0d548bedc46a">How does dependency credit differ from uniform trajectory weighting in GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adepgpo">Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Unit weights do not distinguish supporting actions, final writes, and unrelated commands. DepGPO distributes step credit by traceable writes and distance, then normalizes to preserve token-weighted mean advantage and sign. It depends on tracer accuracy and does not prove causality or individual necessity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An input read followed by an answer write can get indirect credit. Unrelated temporary-file cleanup gets less weight, while negative trajectory advantage stays negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03634">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03634-depgpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-10cd0d548bedc46a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:depgpo" data-paper-title="Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5469b9418d6e2fa5">What boundaries apply to multiple commands per step, missing records, and verifier-generated files?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adepgpo">Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sum command credits within one step, rather than averaging. Missing records or fully tied weights revert to unit weights. Exclude verifier-written resources and stdout values already present in the task prompt; paths and line numbers come from trusted tracing. Local work parses no shell, runs no real Qwen RL, and only verifies the mechanism on four hand-built chains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the grader generates a result file, treating it as an agent write rewards a nonexistent contribution. Remove such artifacts from the tracer input.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 公式与关键区别, 本地复现（机制验证）, 复现边界与下一步. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03634">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03634-depgpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5469b9418d6e2fa5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:adastep" data-paper-title="AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-adastep-2ac090d9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-926133c26eb20165">Why does AdaStep distinguish an action&#x27;s effect from luck in later trajectories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aadastep">AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>At the same intermediate state, later decisions still affect success. Assigning terminal differences directly to the first action is noisy. AdaStep uses multiple observed trajectories to assess local credit reliability, retaining global outcomes while cautiously adjusting step signals. It trains no separate critic and does not prove causal effects from few samples.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After the same lookup, one continuation answers correctly and another transcribes incorrectly. Compare between-action differences with within-action fluctuations rather than blaming the lookup for all variation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03223">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03223-adastep/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-926133c26eb20165">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:adastep" data-paper-title="AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-01ccc5b94842adc5">Why lower local credit correction when within-action return variance is high at the same anchor state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aadastep">AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Random continuations after one action can produce very different outcomes, implying the local action explains little of the variation. Variance decomposition trusts local advantage more when between-action differences dominate; otherwise it preserves global advantage and suppresses the correction. Estimate weights from raw returns rather than arbitrarily normalizing away variance relationships.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If rollouts from both actions A and B produce zeros and perfect scores, continuation randomness dominates. Do not strongly attribute a single outcome to either action.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03223">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03223-adastep/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-01ccc5b94842adc5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:adastep" data-paper-title="AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-064d790622e98c72">How does AdaStep&#x27;s return-statistics approach differ from training a critic for step evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aadastep">AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A critic learns state or action values to organize credit. AdaStep estimates local-correction reliability directly from observed returns for different actions at the same anchor, with no separate critic. It saves a predictor but still needs repeated states and sample coverage. Critic-free does not imply noiseless or universally more accurate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated actions from the same webpage state supply empirical variation. A single occurrence cannot provide a reliable local estimate by itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03223">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03223-adastep/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-064d790622e98c72">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:adastep" data-paper-title="AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f78bea596aecce94">How are few actions, few samples, zero variance, and normalized returns handled?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aadastep">AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Estimate the ratio only with at least two actions, two samples per action, and positive total variance; otherwise use the paper&#x27;s w=1 fallback. Equal returns give zero local advantage. Weight statistics use raw returns, and groups include task IDs to avoid mixing names across tasks. No real environment or policy training ran locally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One action cannot reveal between-action variation, but that does not justify inventing w=0. Identical rewards should not create local correction out of nothing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03223">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.03223-adastep/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f78bea596aecce94">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:graphhca" data-paper-title="GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-graphhca-933790a0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-78177d1580783057">Why does GraphHCA give long-horizon actions a structured training signal before terminal success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agraphhca">GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse terminal feedback can obscure early exploration and key transitions behind one trajectory reward. GraphHCA organizes observed transitions in a graph and propagates success to connected states to estimate action progress. The graph covers observed data only, its potential is not ground truth, and deployment actors cannot see training success labels in advance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If several routes reach success after opening a key door, the graph connects that experience. It cannot assume success behind an unseen door.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.35084-graphhca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-78177d1580783057">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:graphhca" data-paper-title="GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-626bb9e86b51c09f">Why solve a discounted state-graph fixed point before assigning action credit by differences in log potential?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agraphhca">GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Propagate terminal successes and failures as boundary conditions over observed transitions to obtain discounted success potential. Differences in adjacent log potentials turn long-range evidence into local progress, then standardize across actions from a shared state. Complete rollouts support training attribution; do not expose hindsight success boundaries as observations to evaluated agents.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two paths through one intermediate state can share downstream success evidence. Compare whether actions leaving that state approach success or lead toward a dead end.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.35084-graphhca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-626bb9e86b51c09f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:graphhca" data-paper-title="GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7232cac30f7687cb">How do differences in graph potential differ from broadcasting one advantage to the whole trajectory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agraphhca">GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Trajectory advantage does not distinguish steps moving toward promising states. Potential differences highlight improved or worsened state value and are standardized among actions sharing a start. They depend on empirical transition probabilities and ε, not independent causal contribution or guaranteed loop penalties.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>In trajectories with the same terminal result, moving to high potential and returning to low potential can get different local credits instead of one shared value.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.35084-graphhca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7232cac30f7687cb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:graphhca" data-paper-title="GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b3bf6752fef4363f">Why do local Transition and success inputs stay with the estimator rather than the actor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agraphhca">GraphHCA: Closed-Form Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal labels estimate training-side potential. The actor reads only the public state then available, not future success boundaries. No language model was trained or integrated into Evolve. Fixed-point convergence and credit rankings are mechanism evidence; full integration needs real rollouts, updates, and isolated evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Labeling a terminal state after training interaction can help compute credit. Telling a test agent which successor leads to success leaks the result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.35084-graphhca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b3bf6752fef4363f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dr-credit" data-paper-title="Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-dr-credit-775af357" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-525c97d9167576c7">Why does Dr.Credit ask whether each deep-research retrieval adds new evidence for the answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adr-credit">Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An agent can search repeatedly and collect near-duplicates without completing the facts needed. Dr.Credit links process feedback to rubric support so retrieval actually advances the answer. Rewards come from training-side judgments of support, not document counts; judge and rubric reliability still limit credit quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three reposts of a known price do not establish warranty terms. Finding the original warranty can add a missing answer requirement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.34296-dr-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-525c97d9167576c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dr-credit" data-paper-title="Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2a21b47c32a7be2a">Why shouldn&#x27;t retrieving duplicate evidence repeatedly earn the same process reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adr-credit">Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Credit should measure new support relative to accepted evidence, not tool calls. Track historical rubric coverage and score new or partial support to discourage reward farming. Retain outcome advantage so local novelty remains aligned with research goals, and require verifiable support relationships.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retrieving the same date twice earns no full second reward without a new constraint. Finding previously missing affiliation evidence adds support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.34296-dr-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2a21b47c32a7be2a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dr-credit" data-paper-title="Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-db3655f96d65603f">How does incremental rubric-based process feedback differ in timing from grading only the final answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adr-credit">Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal scoring judges the deliverable but cannot easily isolate useful retrievals. Incremental support checks when individual requirements gain evidence and links feedback to those actions. Supported evidence can still be misused in the final answer; neither signal replaces the other, and evaluated actors must not see the training rubric.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A retrieval can find the correct date and complete a process requirement while the final answer copies the year incorrectly. Terminal scoring should still mark that error.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.34296-dr-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-db3655f96d65603f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dr-credit" data-paper-title="Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-15d7ab33e8441f51">What can local fixture rubrics and support scores validate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adr-credit">Dr.Credit: Rubric-Grounded Process Credit Assignment for Deep Research Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They validate history updates, no repeat credit for duplicates, and direction of incremental credit. They do not test whether a semantic judge correctly recognizes support. The policy does not read gold answers, and a three-seed mini-suite is not Deep Research capability. Stronger claims need real sources, trustworthy matching, and actual training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A fixture stating that evidence A supports criterion one can test that the second retrieval adds zero credit. It does not test whether a model recognizes that support on a webpage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.34296-dr-credit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-15d7ab33e8441f51">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dependency-refinement" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-dependency-refinement-97ad396d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4a0523d8d2933e96">Why can&#x27;t long multi-turn training trajectories simply be truncated by length?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adependency-refinement">Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ShanghaiTech University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tool traces depend on observations, reasoning, and actions. Early or long content may support the final conclusion, and mechanical truncation makes later turns inexplicable. Dependency Refinement retains necessary semantic connections while reducing cost. Annotations may be wrong; shorter traces do not prove more learning or that deleted content never matters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the first turn establishes authorized scope and the final action relies on it, keeping only recent messages makes the action appear unsupported.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.18417-dependency-refinement/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4a0523d8d2933e96">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dependency-refinement" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f59aedad5aa4c32a">Why prune leaves first when compressing multi-turn traces instead of deleting the longest message?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adependency-refinement">Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ShanghaiTech University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A dependency DAG marks turns supporting the final answer; leaves are more likely to be redundant branches with no downstream dependency. Strict and then relaxed merging reduce repetition while preserving required information flow. The longest message may contain the key tool evidence, so length-only pruning can remove necessary causal context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A long log may contain the only error code, while short chat has no dependents. Prune the chat leaf rather than discarding the log because it is longer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.18417-dependency-refinement/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f59aedad5aa4c32a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:dependency-refinement" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-79061bfab7fe97d2">How do leaf pruning and turn merging differ in semantic preservation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adependency-refinement">Dependency-Aware Trajectory Refinement for Efficient Multi-Turn Agent Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ShanghaiTech University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pruning removes branches that no longer serve the objective. Merging compactly represents steps that can be expressed together. Strict merging applies tighter constraints; relaxed merging seeks more compression at greater risk. Preserve order and dependency invariants instead of substituting arbitrary summaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two reads of identical state can be merged. Keep the causal order between a change and verification, not a vague &#x27;handled&#x27; summary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.18417-dependency-refinement/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-79061bfab7fe97d2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
